10 Things I Hate About You, directed by Gil Junger, follows teen Joey who wants to date Bianca, but she can’t date until her antisocial older sister, Kat, has a boyfriend, per her strict father’s rules. That’s when Joey pays a mysterious boy, Patrick, to ask Kat out.

articles.title: James Bond Auction: Daniel Craig’s ‘Skyfall’ Suit, Ana de Armas’ ‘No Time to Die’ Dress Hitting Block
articles.author: Ryan Gajewski

paras.en: James Bond fans are likely to be shaken by an auction set to honor the beloved franchise.

Propstore’s online Bond auction features 400 lots spanning every film in the long-running series and highlighting the franchise’s evolution, from 1962’s Dr. No through 2021’s No Time to Die. The James Bond Online Auction is now available for worldwide bids, which can be placed through the auction link, and it runs until Oct. 27.

The auction’s highlights include Daniel Craig‘s Tom Ford suit, shirt and cufflinks from 2012’s Skyfall, expected to sell for as much as $53,000. Also hitting the block are Ana de Armas‘ Paloma dress and sandals from No Time to Die, with the outfit likely to go for around $53,000.

One lucky bidder will end up with a set of 14 first-edition books by Bond author Ian Fleming, with the collection from publishing firm Jonathan Cape expected to sell for upwards of $50,000. A linen-backed British quad poster for Dr. No is valued at as much as $22,000, while a clapperboard from 1983’s Octopussy could be headed for a sale above $10,000.

“James Bond has a unique place in popular culture, and interest remains strong to this day,” Propstore director of consignments Alastair McCrea tells The Hollywood Reporter. “Bond has been part of cinema for over 60 years, with each generation having its own Bond, its own favorite film and memorable moments. One person grew up with Sean Connery, another with Pierce Brosnan, another with Daniel Craig, so you can still have three generations of the same family debating over who the best 007 is. That’s what makes collecting Bond so appealing; there’s something for everyone, whether it’s the films, the actors, the gadgets, posters, costumes or the original artwork. Very few film franchises can claim that, and it’s a big part of why the collecting market remains so strong.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This follows Propstore’s previous online auction that featured more than 300 items from director Denis Villeneuve‘s Blade Runner 2049. That auction concluded last week, with such highlights as the signature coat worn by Ryan Gosling, which sold for $201,600, including the buyer’s premium. This Bond-focused sale takes place as anticipation builds amid the ongoing casting process for the star of the next 007 movie that Villeneuve is set to direct.

“The news about a new movie on the horizon always piques renewed interest, and I expect that to grow over the forthcoming years,” adds McCrea. “The links to other brands have also kept the interest high, from Aston Martin to Omega, and they all add to the exposure. The Daniel Craig era saw the biggest price rise in collectables, and this can be seen across the areas of posters, scripts, books and costumes.”

articles.title: Australian data center operator NextDC's shares plunge 40% after it slashes earnings forecast

paras.en: Shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast, citing power supply delays at its Melbourne facility amid local community and stakeholder opposition.

The company lowered its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to between $475 million Australian dollars and A$500 million, from A$615 million to A$640 million forecast earlier, while cutting its underlying earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, or EBITDA, forecast to A$245 million to A$265 million from A$385 million to A$410 million.

The delays to power stem from the suspension of infrastructure upgrades at the company's M3 Melbourne data center amid community opposition, with electricity distributor Jemena not expecting to resume work before February 2027, according to NextDC.
Jemena cited safety concerns and restricted access to work sites due to community opposition, as well as a lack of consent from the local council pending further community consultation.
Citi said in a note that NextDC's power delays could affect earnings beyond fiscal 2027, citing delays to approvals for the M3 expansion and a longer-than-expected timeline for transformer upgrades.

As Australia grapples with growing concerns over the impact of data center developments on local communities, Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government was working to establish national standards for investment.

Chalmers told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Wednesday that the government welcomes investment in data centers and AI infrastructure, provided it aligns with the country's national interest, adding that the government was finalizing national investment standards to address concerns surrounding AI deployment.

Australia is not alone in facing opposition to data center projects, there has been growing push back against data center developments worldwide, amid concerns over their impact on local communities and the environment.
NextDC shares have declined for seven straight weeks, and are on course to end lower for the eighth week.

articles.title: U.S. eyes refining muscle of Indian billionaire Ambani's Reliance as Rubio visits Jamnagar plant

paras.en: U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will discuss refining Western energy supplies with Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries when he visits the company's plant in Jamnagar, Gujarat — the world's largest single-site refinery.

The U.S. is looking to "work together more closely" with Reliance for refining energy from the "Western Hemisphere," Rubio said in an interview with India's Network 18, which is owned by Reliance. "I think that's helpful to India, but it's also helpful to us," he added.

Reliance's Jamnagar refinery, which Rubio will visit on Wednesday, has a crude processing capacity of 1.4 million barrels per day. Reliance has also emerged as the biggest buyer of Venezuelan crude outside of the U.S., as of end-September.
The company's "extraordinary" refining capacity could help India diversify its energy supplies, Rubio said, hinting at possibly greater offtake of Venezuelan crude.

"We think there's an opportunity for them [Reliance Industries] to continue to help India diversify its supply chain, its supply of energy," Rubio said, adding that Venezuela was ramping up energy production, and that "India has had a long history of being able to refine some of that."

U.S. President Donald Trump has been pushing India to buy more Venezuelan oil to replace Russian barrels, and while state-owned oil companies are making opportunistic purchases, Reliance has been the primary buyer.

Beyond oil purchases, Reliance has been deepening ties with the U.S. this year, with Trump announcing in March that America will build its first new oil refinery in 50 years, helped by investment from Ambani's Reliance.
While Reliance has not confirmed the size of investment, Trump in a Truth Social post had said that "THIS IS A HISTORIC $300 BILLION DOLLAR DEAL — THE BIGGEST IN U.S. HISTORY."

Reliance has never made an announcement about the refinery investment, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC, adding that it creates an air of uncertainty around the deal. Rubio would seek to "clinch" that deal or take it a little further, Chaudhuri said.
Rubio told Network 18 that Reliance had "invested in increasing the refining capacity within the United States."

His visit to Jamnagar also comes at a time when diesel prices have surged in the U.S., with midterm elections looming. Diesel prices, which affect American truckers, farmers, and shippers, are expected to remain elevated going into next year.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Rubio underscored Reliance's ability to refine heavy crude and referred to India as a "refining superpower" when asked about the role New Delhi and its companies can play in meeting the world's energy demand.
Indian and Chinese refineries are good at handling heavy and medium-heavy crude from Venezuela and Russia, Chaudhuri said, adding that this grade of fuel is better-suited for producing diesel.

articles.title: Stock futures rise as traders evaluate latest raft of earnings; SpaceX shares surge: Live updates

paras.en: U.S. stock futures were up early Wednesday as traders weighed the latest round of earnings reports.
S&P 500 futures gained 0.29% and Nasdaq-100 futures added 0.7%. Dow futures were flat.

In Asia, South Korea's Kospi advanced 2.7%, rebounding from Tuesday's losses. Japan's Nikkei 225 was up 0.8%. The Hang Seng index declined 0.35%, while mainland China was flat. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was little changed.

Shares of Elon Musk's SpaceX jumped 8% after the company said its revenue grew 161% in the third quarter. Musk also said that SpaceX and Tesla, his auto manufacturer, have formed special committees to discuss a merger. Tesla shares were up 1%.

In regular trading, the Dow Industrials advanced nearly 530 points, or 1%, buoyed by a post-earnings jump in 3M. Shares gained more than 5% after the industrial products company raised its full-year guidance for profit. The S&P 500 gained 0.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite ended the session marginally lower.
Oil prices ended the session slightly lower. West Texas Intermediate crude futures slipped 1.8% on the day, while Brent crude futures lost 0.7%.
This earnings season could help propel stocks as the year winds down, according to Christian Mueller-Glissmann, head of asset allocation for Goldman Sachs Research.

"Near term there might be more volatility due to [artificial intelligence] concerns, Middle East tensions and midterm elections, but we think earnings support with lighter positioning and lower valuations should help equities into year-end," he wrote in a note.

Concerns around the sustainability of the AI trade have weighed on market sentiment, with traders focusing on debt-backed AI investments and whether the infrastructure demand justifies companies' spending. Data storage play Seagate Technology added 2% in Tuesday's regular trading, while neocloud stock CoreWeave advanced more than 1%.

On Wednesday, investors can expect some more insight into the AI trade, with Meta Platforms due to report after the bell. Earlier this month, the company rolled out its latest AI model, Muse Wonder, which is only available to paying users.
Traders are also watching for results from Tesla, IBM and Southwest Airlines, all due Wednesday.

articles.title: Math Puzzle: Baby bottle mix-up

paras.en: This problem is the result of many hours of cleaning baby bottles for two daughters. Suppose your baby uses a certain type of bottle that is composed of three pieces (say, top, middle and bottom). The bottles come in two colors (say, blue and green). You have three blue bottles and two green bottles, for a total of five bottles. Your baby uses all five bottles in a single day. Because you’re perpetually tired, you do not disassemble and wash the bottles until the end of the day. After the bottles have dried overnight, you reassemble them and begin your next day. Such is the life of a new parent.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When you go to reassemble the bottles, you notice that you can exchange parts among them so that some are “mixed up.” For example, you can put a green top on a blue middle and blue bottom. Naturally, you try your hand at swapping parts so there is no complete bottle of a single color—in other words, you find a “derangement” of the bottles.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Suppose you then buy some new bottles in a third color (say, pink). What is the minimum number of pink bottles required to ensure that no derangement can occur?
Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. And it costs money. That’s why I and the journalists here at Scientific American hope you’ll join our community.
Jeanna Bryner, Editor in Chief, Scientific American

articles.title: The mathematical impossibility of making a perfect world map

paras.en: On September 4, 2026, the United Nations adopted a resolution to promote a new map of the world. The resolution encourages governments, schools and organizations to replace the much-criticized Mercator projection, which significantly overestimates the size of countries and continents near the poles, with the area-preserving Equal Earth projection developed in 2018.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

The move sparked a lot of chatter. Some called the decision a step to dismantle “cartographic colonialism,” others a “radical ideological project.” In total, 164 nations voted in favor of the proposal, six abstained, and the U.S. was the only country to vote against. The resolution is not legally binding, but it sends a clear signal to use a fairer (and more accurate) representation of our world in the future.

Creating a suitable map of Earth might not sound too difficult at first. But mathematics makes it an unsolvable problem: a sphere cannot be mapped onto a flat plane. Try to wrap a spherical object in gift paper, for instance, and you will inevitably crease the paper. Cartographers have been aware of this challenge for centuries. It is impossible to design a world map that accurately depicts both the precise shape of the continents and countries and their area simultaneously. Compromises—and heated debates—are unavoidable.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: In 1569 scholar Gerardus Mercator developed a projection, now named after him, that accurately depicts angles on a sphere. With this approach, all continents and countries retain their shape, which is particularly advantageous for seafarers. Using a Mercator projection, a compass course corresponds to a straight line on the map. For centuries, this world map was the standard.

To obtain the Mercator projection, a cylindrical map is placed around Earth so that it touches the globe along the equator. Then every point on Earth is projected onto the cylinder from Earth’s center. The result is that countries near the poles are enlarged such that Greenland (836,330 square miles) and Africa (11.7 million square miles) appear roughly the same size on this map—even though Africa is 14 times as large.

In the 20th century, German historian Arno Peters objected to the Eurocentric worldview and the ways this map contributed to it. He called for a new representation and, in 1973, designed an equal-area projection. Technically cartographer James Gall developed a similar world map a century earlier, but it received little attention at the time.

To obtain this Gall–Peters projection, a cylindrical map is used, similar to the Mercator projection. In this case, however, the points of the globe are not projected onto the map from Earth’s center but along horizontal lines. The result is an equal-area representation: the sizes of the countries on the globe correspond to those on the map.

But critics raised several objections to this map, including the significant distortions to the shapes of countries and continents. Countries in low latitudes become especially warped in this presentation.

In March 2017 the Boston public school system announced its intention to replace its Mercator projection maps with the Gall-Peters projection. In response, software developer Bojan Šavrič of the Californian company Esri and cartographers Tom Patterson of the U.S. National Park Service and Bernhard Jenny of Monash University in Australia began searching for more suitable equal-area projections. And when they could not find an option that met all of their aesthetic criteria, they decided to develop something new that they called Equal Earth.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The researchers based their work on the Robinson projection, developed in the early 1960s. This is a variant of the world map that is neither area-preserving nor angle-preserving. Unlike the previously mentioned examples, it does not correspond to a mathematical projection, meaning it has no underlying formulas that generate it. Instead it is constructed using a table of empirically determined reference points. The points in between these reference points are determined by interpolation. While this may seem unscientific, the result appears natural: the Robinson map only shows significant deviations in angle and area in the polar regions.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Šavrič, Patterson and Jenny aimed to create a similarly natural effect but wanted to preserve the area of various landmasses. In 2018 they published their Equal Earth map in the International Journal of Geographical Information Science. It is a pseudocylindrical projection: Latitude lines are represented as straight lines, as in ordinary cylindrical projections, but longitude lines are not (except for the prime meridian).

They determined the details of the new world map in two steps: First, the researchers combined two existing projections using custom-developed graphics software. This visual approach allowed them to create a subjectively appealing appearance for the coordinate grid and the continental landmasses. The second step involved calculating the corresponding projection equations.

“Generally speaking, there are no truly ‘perfect’ maps,” cartographer Lorenz Hurni of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich told Swiss broadcaster SRF. “This map seeks a compromise to minimize the distortion of the shapes of countries and continents.” That’s why many countries—including members of the African Union—consider it the best possible representation of a world map. The state of Togo therefore introduced the new resolution at the United Nations, entitled “Correct the Map,” on its behalf in an aim to establish the Equal Earth map as the standard.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Although the U.N. flag uses a completely different representation of the world (an equidistant azimuthal projection that has been artistically corrected along the lines of latitude), many hope that the U.N. resolution will gradually be implemented throughout the world, updating the way we look at it.

articles.title: Christina Applegate says she was misdiagnosed with MS—how could that happen?

paras.en: Actress Christina Applegate’s announcement on Tuesday that she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) in 2021 immediately made headlines. Her experience, while not the norm, is far from unusual, experts say.

Applegate disclosed the revelation on an episode of her podcast with Jamie Lynn Sigler, MeSsy, which centers on their lives with MS. (Sigler disclosed that she has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, or RRMS, in 2016.) “In January of 2021, I had numbness in my toes, and that numbness grew to all of my legs,” Applegate recalled on the podcast. “And then the pain started.”
After rounds of tests for a variety of conditions, her doctor found “almost 40” lesions on her brain and diagnosed her with MS, she said.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

MS can be devastating. The neurological condition causes the body’s immune system to attack the nervous system, including parts of the brain. Symptoms can include fatigue, mood changes, dizziness, vision issues and numbness in the arms and legs.
Now, five years later, Applegate said that, after analyzing brain scans with a “new technology,” her doctor told her she doesn’t have MS. “I’m back at square one,” she said.
Her experience is more common than you might think.

“Diagnosing MS is a little bit like putting a puzzle together,” says Bruce Bebo, chief research and medical affairs officer at the National Multiple Sclerosis Society. “There’s not a single diagnostic test that tells you, ‘You have MS.’” The disease’s symptoms overlap with other conditions, such as neuromyelitis optica, which have to be ruled out before a diagnosis can be made.

Estimates vary, but a recent meta-analysis found that around 15 percent of MS cases across studies were misdiagnoses. The absolute odds of a misdiagnosis can vary by patient population and clinical setting, however, Bebo says. For instance, a study performed at a patient referral center where MS patients have been sent for additional analysis may inherently show higher rates of misdiagnosis in that patient population, says Thomas Flagiello, a neurologist at NYU Langone.
Overall, “although misdiagnosis happens, the majority of cases are correctly diagnosed,” Flagiello says.

Diagnostic tools are getting better. In 2025 the International Advisory Committee on Clinical Trials in Multiple Sclerosis updated its guidelines on how to diagnose MS to reflect recent advancements, including the ability to look in brain scans for specific clues, such as the central vein sign, a small vein running through brain lesions, or a specific kind of brain feature called a paramagnetic rim lesion, Bebo says.
Identifying these markers in patients’ brains could help reduce misdiagnoses, Bebo says. But as of now, it’s impossible to totally rule out a misdiagnosis.
As Applegate’s story illustrates, the consequences of a misdiagnosis can be substantial. It could mean someone receives treatment they don’t need—or misses out on treatment that they do, Bebo says.

That’s why getting a diagnosis right “really matters,” Bebo says. “Whether you have MS or you ultimately have some other condition, people experiencing significant neurologic symptoms deserve to have a careful evaluation.”

articles.title: Can math stay human in the age of AI?
articles.author: Kathryn Hulick

paras.en: “Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.

The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.

This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?

Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.

The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.

“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”

In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.

The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.

But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”

The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.

The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math. But there is widespread concern, she says, that AI models have accessed people’s unpublished work. “We had a healthy, collaborative, sharing culture that is being destroyed,” she says. “Now, people are wary of sharing their ideas.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Not all mathematicians feel this way about AI. The technology is “making math more accessible,” says Andrew Turner, who wonders why a small group of mathematicians should get to decide how we solve problems. Turner, who studied math and physics and is Now CTO of the company Plasma AI, based in New York City thinks “math is becoming engineering.” And doing math with machines will allow people to “answer questions previously unfathomable.”
A few days after Bloom shut down the competition on his website, Plasma AI announced a new website to track progress on Erdős problems. They will welcome AI results.

Bloom doesn’t see math as a Silicon Valley–esque move-fast-and-break-things competition. I agree, and hope that curious people will continue to explore problems they care about, with AI helping rather than taking over. At the end of his post announcing the changes to his website, Bloom wrote something that makes me tear up every time I read it. I hope everyone, even the most enthusiastic AI users, can find the time for this type of work: “Be confused, be stuck, be inspired. Find a messy proof, then find a better one,” he wrote. “Get tired, get hungry, get into a flow state. Argue, laugh, give up, drink some coffee and attack it again. Be human. Let your brain be open.”

articles.title: Artemis II results show how much science people can do at the moon
articles.author: Lisa Grossman

paras.en: Six months after the Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon, the value of their closeup view is coming into focus. The first science results, released on October 7, reveal details of the moon’s array of colors, how often it gets hit by tiny rocks and lessons for squeezing as much science as possible out of future human lunar missions.

“We worked extremely hard to make sure we were able to maximize lunar science return from wherever we could in this mission,” said Artemis II flight science operations lead Kelsey Young at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting on October 7. “This is creating yet another tool in our toolbox as planetary scientists to understand our moon, our solar system, even our own planet.”

NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon in April — the first time humans had been anywhere near our natural satellite in more than 50 years. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen spent about seven hours in close proximity to the moon taking scientific observations, describing the moon’s surprising colors and textures and witnessing a solar eclipse from space.

Almost all of that event was livestreamed. But the astronauts took thousands of photos, notes and audio recordings that weren’t immediately made public. Part of the science team’s job was to digest those observations and release the data to anyone who wants to study them within six months of splashdown on April 10.

With three days to spare, the team released three reports and a massive data archive on October 7, the 67th anniversary of when the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft took the first photograph of the farside of the moon. The results offer a rare test of what trained human observers can add to lunar research and what NASA can learn for future missions to the lunar surface.

“We’re really excited to release all of this data,” earth scientist Sara Schmidt of NASA Johnson Space flight Cener in Houston said during the meeting. After six months of hard work, “this is enabling science to happen for the next, I don’t know, 60 years, if not more.”
How astronauts learn to observe the moon
Surprisingly, the most valuable data from the mission were not the mind-blowingly gorgeous photos, but the astronauts’ verbal and written descriptions of what they were seeing.

Before launch, the astronauts had extensive training in lunar geology and science observations. They were an extension of the science team, said field geologist Cindy Evans also of NASA Johnson Space Flight Center, one of the astronauts’ instructors.
“You could hear it in their voices. They understood the language of geology,” she said.
That training was meant to help answer a question Young hears often: What can humans add that a camera can’t?

During the flyby, the astronauts worked in pairs. Two of them spoke to mission control on the ground, giving periodic updates to the science team on what they were seeing. The other two recorded themselves describing their observations and reactions and used a stylus to annotate specially made maps of the moon that had been uploaded to their tablets during flight. Those notes, doodles and recordings were not made public until now.
The idea was to give the crew high tech field notebooks, Young says.

“If you have any field experience, you know your field notebook is your best friend,” she said in the meeting. On Earth, geologists capture nuance and context in written and spoken words, as well as sketches, she said. “We wanted to provide the ability to capture that nuanced information from the crew.”
One example of this was when Koch sketched her view of the Orientale basin, detailing differences in texture and layers around the crater.
“Sketches can be so powerful,” Young says. “They’re quick and dirty and that’s exactly the right thing to do. You’re capturing that nuance really quickly before it leaves your brain.”

Some of the most unique observations came during the 54 minutes when the moon eclipsed the sun, giving the astronauts a view of the solar corona, interplanetary dust and other stars and planets. That was a favorite moment for planetary scientist Jennifer Heldmann of NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.

“That audio showed their sheer joy and amazement in what they were seeing and where they were,” Heldmann says. “They were so blown away by what they were seeing, while also taking very relevant science observations.”
But some of the most affecting moments were when words failed. When Glover and Koch saw the Earth emerge from behind the moon, for a while all they could say was “Oh my gosh!”
“I guess I should be trying to describe it, but I mean, good grief,” Glover’s tablet recorded him saying.
“No, I tried, but it’s impossible,” Koch agreed. “You might be able to fly a spaceship and talk, but if you can see that and talk, you just ain’t right.”
Astronauts spotted tiny impacts on the moon
Another thing the astronauts were able to see during the eclipse were impact flashes — tiny blips of light marking where bits of rock hit the moon.
“It’s a pinpoint of light,” Hansen said in his recorded observations. “It’s not like a meteor, you didn’t see anything else, it’s just like a bloop.”

Before launch, the science team identified and prioritized observations they hoped the crew would be able to make during the flyby. Impact flashes were at the top of the list. Seeing the flashes would give scientists a way to estimate how often the moon is struck by incoming rocks, and how large those rocks are. That’s an important thing to know for protecting future missions where astronauts will walk on the surface or build a long-term moon base.

Scientists didn’t know whether the astronauts would see any flashes at all. They saw five. The flashes were “pinpricks of light lasting less than a second, with no color associated with the flash,” Heldmann said at the meeting.

Comparing the number of flashes per minute to theoretical models of how many impacts the moon might experience, scientists determined that the incoming rocks were tiny, about 8.5 grams and just over 4.5 centimeters across — about the size of a golf ball.
“With these observations, we believe that the Artemis II crew set a record for the smallest meteorites ever optically observed to impact the moon,” Heldmann said.
The resulting craters are probably less than a meter wide, too small for cameras on NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to see.

That’s good news for future astronauts. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is supposed to bring astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since Apollo. If successful, it will be a two-week mission using landers from spaceflight companies Blue Origin or SpaceX. The probability of dangerous impact during such a mission is less than 1 in 10 million, Heldmann said. For a larger moon base meant to last a decade, the probability is higher, but still low.
“Now we can start to quantify those impact probabilities, which turns out are very very low,” she says. “Crews will be very safe.”

The moon’s muted colors were another high-priority observation for the science team. Lunar hues and brightnesses can change with terrain roughness, surface temperature and mineralogy — and they’re much more discernable with human eyes than with cameras. The crew also saw how colors changed as the viewing angle and light levels changed.
“This is such a cool demonstration of the value of human eyes as scientific sensors,” said planetary scientist Ariel Deutsch, also of NASA Ames.

Combining the crew’s observations with other data going back to the 1970s let scientists connect colors to composition. Blues were associated with titanium-rich volcanic rocks. Browns reflect different iron levels. Greens are from glass formed during volcanic eruptions or asteroid impacts.
Future astronauts could use this information to create terrain maps and to find specific materials on the moon for sample collection or resources.
The crew also was enamored with the terminator, the boundary between light and dark, which revealed lunar topography in a new way.

“Even as rugged as the far side looks … man, when you look at the terminator, it is just, like, impossibly rugged,” Wiseman said during the flight. “And it reminds you that the whole farside is that way. It’s just the terminator is really bringing out the shadows and the hills and the valleys. And it is just — it’s unbelievable.”
The lighting at the terminator is similar to what future astronauts might expect at the moon’s south pole, where the sun will be low on the horizon and may cast dramatic shadows.
“We want to make sure we have a good handle on that for both science and operations and exploration,” Heldmann said.
What Artemis II taught NASA for future moon missions
With the lessons from Artemis II in hand, now it’s the next astronauts’ turn.

Some recommendations coming out of Artemis II focus on improving conditions in the spacecraft and weaving science into mission planning better. For example, due to time constraints, the astronauts’ cameras were not calibrated before flight. The team is now trying to calibrate them back on Earth, but it can’t re-create how the windows affected images because the windows were charred on the way back through Earth’s atmosphere.

Another takeaway from Artemis II is to continue to refine and train astronauts in descriptive notetaking. The audio notes will be even more important for the first landed missions, where astronauts in spacesuits will not be able to write in a notebook.
“We want to train astronauts to be field scientists, regardless of the landing site, regardless of the mission that they’re given,” Young says.
The buddy system of two astronauts at the windows, two talking to the ground, led to better science, the team concluded.

“The crew had scientific discussions and tried to understand what they were viewing,” Heldmann says. For surface missions, where time is limited and choices must be made quickly, that collaboration will be even more important.
The crew also commented on how helpful it was.

“When we actually do go down there to the surface, I know for safety reasons that we would never send someone alone, but I just want to really emphasize how important the discussion time was,” Glover said. “When we started to talk, we not only got better science discussion, we got better human connection.”

articles.title: Rule breaking by just a few people can be contagious
articles.author: Sujata Gupta

paras.en: On the long drive to my kid’s sporting event this weekend, most drivers, myself included, cruised a few miles over the speed limit. A few drivers, though, blazed past in the left lane. Mindful of safety — and police cruisers — I didn’t follow suit.

Left unchecked though, a few bad actors can trigger social breakdown, researchers report October 21 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The truly deviant among us “basically take off the guardrails of the group,” says Lucas Molleman, a psychologist at the University of Amsterdam.

Molleman and his colleagues designed a thought experiment to show what it takes to sway people to bend or break the rules. They picked a contentious time: A week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election. The team recruited 750 U.S. participants, with roughly half identifying as Democrats and half as Republicans. The online participants watched an animated shooting star streak across a row of 100 squares and then selected which square shone the brightest.

Though the brightest square always appeared around the row’s middle, participants received more money for selecting squares farther to the right (the farthest-right square netted participants roughly the equivalent of $1.30). Dedicated rule followers, or those who always followed the rules, and rule breakers, existed in roughly equal numbers, with each comprising about a fifth of the larger group, initial tests showed.

The researchers then stirred the pot. Participants repeated the simple experiment several times while receiving information about a previous respondent, including their political affiliation and level of adherence to the rule. Rule followers rarely begot more rule followers, even when respondents belonged to the same political party, the team found.

The reverse held true for rule breakers, though. Receiving information that someone with the same political leanings had just disregarded the rules shifted selections rightward on average. Absent social cues, participants selected the farthest-right square roughly 23 percent of the time. That increased to almost 40 percent of the time after participants learned that a political comrade had made the most lucrative choice. Bad behavior, in other words, was contagious.
Most individuals’ rule-breaking levels mirrored or stayed below that of others. But just over 4 percent of individuals escalated deviant behavior beyond that of the previous respondent.

The researchers then created a computer simulation to see how those rule-breaking behaviors might play out across time. They designed a digital twin for each of the 750 participants and had the doppelgängers interact in groups of 100. In some scenarios, those few escalation-prone individuals could push everyone in the group toward wild rule breaking. But if the 100-twin selection had the same proportion of dedicated rule followers as the human experiment, overall deviance settled at a more intermediate level.

paras.en: This study provides some keen insights into how humans might behave absent consequences, says behavioral economist Eugen Dimant of the University of Pennsylvania. “But that’s not how the world works.” His work suggests that to truly understand social contagion and the emergence of mobs, researchers must consider societal forces, such as punishments and social norms, that tend to keep behavior in check.

To Molleman, though, the study’s insights into individual behaviors are key. This pared-down experiment shows how just a few bad actors can cause entire groups to spiral out of control. Such findings could underpin everything from collective speeding to peaceful protests that turn violent, he says. “This is fundamental science … Obviously reality is way more complex.”

articles.title: Researchers Identify New 'Circadian' Subtype of Depression Affecting 1 in 4 Patients
articles.author: Jess Cockerill

paras.en: Many people with depression don't respond to existing treatments, and scientists think it might be because of the many different routes people can take to arrive at the same depressive symptoms.
A new study found a quarter of patients fit into a 'circadian' subtype of depression, arising from a state of perpetual jet lag.
Led by psychiatry researchers Jacob Crouse and Ian Hickie, a team from the University of Sydney in Australia has published its findings in the British Journal of Psychiatry.

Current clinical guidelines treat depression as one disorder. But Hickie and team believe that while depression may look similar for each patient, many different biological problems may be driving the symptoms.
Most available treatments for depression assume the disorder is underpinned by anxiety. But for the 30 percent of young people with atypical depression, that is not the case.
So, Hickie asks, if it's not underpinned by anxiety, then what is driving it?
"What we've been investigating for some time now is the neurobiology of the brain regulators of the circadian system," he says.
The circadian systems in our body are those that are aligned with the 24-hour day and night cycle, with light being the main signal modulating these systems. But every body is a little bit different.
"The co-ordination of those clocks underpins your mood, your metabolism, your concentration, your sleep/wake cycle, and many other key factors," Hickie explains.
"When it's off, you feel jet-lagged all the time. You feel tired, you feel exhausted, you gain weight, you can't concentrate, you sleep poorly, and your behavior changes."

Hickie and his colleagues have now found evidence that this basic mechanism does indeed underlie a proportion of mood disorders, in data from 11,380 participants in the ongoing Australian Genetics of Depression Study.
The researchers define the circadian subtype of depression with six criteria.

For someone with circadian depression, their symptoms will change with the seasons, due to the shifting day lengths. Secondly, the midpoint of their sleep is delayed compared to the general population.

They also experience social jet lag: that is, their sleep midpoint on working days is several hours different than the midpoint on non-working days (i.e., their sleep tendencies do not match the timing that society is typically designed around).

They have an evening chronotype, and when given the opportunity, they will sleep longer than the typical person (perhaps, the researchers suggest, because of the constant experience of jet lag). Unsurprisingly, they also report being very tired in the morning.
Among the 11,380 people included in this study, about 1 in 4 patients fit into this circadian subtype.

There was some overlap with other proposed depression subtypes. The greatest crossover was with atypical depression, but even then, about 1,400 cases met the criteria for atypical depression but not the circadian subtype, which suggests these may still be distinct forms of the disorder.

"Depression is not a uniform illness and understanding the characteristics of different subtypes mean that we can give people earlier access to treatments that will be most effective for them," explains Emiliana Tonini, first author on the new paper.
Participants with the circadian subtype started experiencing depression earlier in life and reported more severe clinical features like mania, psychosis, and suicidality.

They were also more likely to experience weight gain during depressive episodes. They also had a higher genetic risk for major neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD, and inflammatory and cardiovascular health problems.
These participants were also less likely to find common antidepressant medications effective, and tended to experience more side effects from the medications.

"Because circadian depression is linked to people's internal body clock, treatments targeting the circadian rhythm, such as light therapy and melatonin, may be much more relevant, and clinicians should reach for these much earlier in people with this presentation," Crouse says.
"For those who find that antidepressants are not working for them, it is important to speak to your clinician for advice about your individual circumstances."
If this story has raised concerns or you need to talk to someone, please consult this list to find a 24/7 crisis hotline in your country, and reach out for help.
The research has been published in British Journal of Psychiatry.

articles.title: The Way You Sleep Can Reveal Your Risk of Heart Failure Up to 10 Years in Advance
articles.author: Carly Cassella

paras.en: Your dreams may not foretell the future, but the way that your heart falls asleep just might.
Researchers have now shown that in the early stages of sleep, as the nervous system undergoes rapid changes, the heart's electrical activity can be used to determine future health risks.
All that is needed is the data from one electrocardiogram (ECG) lead, placed on the chest during sleep.
With that, artificial intelligence can predict someone's risk of an irregular heartbeat, stroke, heart failure, or death from any cause in the next 10 years.
The findings are published in the journal SLEEP, with support from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH).

"This new approach has the potential to identify individuals at risk for cardiovascular disease years before clinical symptoms arise," says David Goff, acting director of NIH's National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI).
"Evaluating whether this information improves traditional risk prediction is an important next step."
The research team, led by scientists at Emory University, first trained a deep learning system on the public health data of nearly 16,000 patients.
These patients were enrolled in a sleep study at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, and as part of the trial, they had their heart activity measured during sleep by an ECG.

Once trained, the AI system was then put to the test on two more datasets, including nearly 10,000 patients from Emory University Hospital and 13,000 patients from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston.
In the end, the model was able to sort participants into different levels of long-term cardiovascular risk.
After adjusting for conventional risk factors and sleep characteristics, the AI system could predict the 10-year risk of several cardiovascular outcomes.
For each standard deviation increase in the AI's risk score, there was a 103 to 172 percent higher risk of atrial fibrillation, which is an irregular heartbeat.
There was also a 19 to 40 percent higher risk of stroke, a 69 to 133 percent higher risk of heart failure, and a 65 to 82 percent higher risk of death from any cause.
Only one group showed a significantly increased risk of future myocardial infarction, or heart attack.

"Importantly, we found that adding the score from our deep learning model improved prediction of cardiac outcomes beyond established risk factors," says Gari Clifford, study author and professor of biomedical engineering at Georgia Institute of Technology.
"Adding these scores into sleep studies has great potential for improving early detection of cardiovascular disease, determining who is most at risk, and being more proactive in patient care."
Issues with sleep, like insomnia, are known risk factors for cardiovascular disease.
During a polysomnography (PSG) test, which is the gold standard for diagnosing sleep disorders, the heart is often recorded as well.
But unless this data throws up a serious red flag, the findings are rarely considered.
All that subtle information on cardiac function could be going to waste.
Traditional models for cardiovascular risk usually consider ECG recordings when a person is awake or walking.
But during sleep, they may also record important fluctuations.
Using a deep learning algorithm, researchers in the US have now found that ECG recordings show strong predictive value for cardiovascular health outcomes when combined with sleep stages.
That's true even when adjusting for other cardiovascular risk factors, such as age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, and smoking.
During the lightest stage of sleep, for instance, changes to heart rate patterns and electrical conduction seem to be especially indicative of future health risks.
"These rapid autonomic fluctuations may amplify subtle abnormalities in heart-rate dynamics or conduction patterns," the authors explain.

In fact, incorporating ECG-derived data from sleep improved current cardiovascular risk models by up to 6 percent for atrial fibrillation, up to 9 percent for heart failure, and up to 7 percent for mortality prediction.
These absolute increases might seem modest, the authors explain, but they still improve our ability to separate individuals who do and do not develop heart failure beyond traditional means.
With continued development, the AI system has the potential to help health practitioners screen for patients with sleep disorders who may be at extra risk of heart failure.

"In the future, proven analytical approaches like this could be integrated into existing diagnostic tests for patients undergoing sleep studies as a screening tool for multiple adverse cardiovascular outcomes," says Goff.
The research has been published in SLEEP.

articles.title: A Strange New Time Crystal Emerges From Synchronized Vibrations
articles.author: Michelle Starr

paras.en: To us mortals, the flow of time goes one way.
Yesterday is gone, tomorrow is yet to come, and no matter how precisely and faithfully a clock marks the passing seconds, we can never return to a moment that has passed.
But for a time crystal, things are very different.

The constituent ranks of this mysterious state of matter – be they atoms, sound waves, or topological defects – are strictly regimented in time, a repeating pattern of beats that could be snipped from a recording at regular intervals and perfectly superimposed, one over another.
Once thought impossible, time crystals have been observed in systems from physical atomic lattices to levitating styrofoam.

Now, physicists have discovered a strange new way for a time crystal to emerge – not through the imposition of an external rhythm, but through a spontaneous process in which competing vibrations gradually fall into step – order gradually emerging from chaos.

Using a 3D-printed two-dimensional metamaterial, an international team of physicists led by Jonas Veenstra of the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands observed small, rapid vibrations giving way to progressively larger, slower waves, until the entire structure was moving in synchrony.
The researchers call this process "wave coarsening", and it could reveal a new way for matter to organize itself into persistent patterns in time.
One of the biggest challenges to time crystal research is how devastatingly fragile these systems can be.

When you're trying to keep something in very precise step, even a slight disturbance can send it tumbling into disorder. In systems with only one or two spatial dimensions, those disturbances can be particularly destructive.
This makes the emergence of a stable, synchronized rhythm in a two-dimensional material especially intriguing.
One possible route to such order lies in the way different parts of a material interact with each other.
Veenstra and his colleagues wanted to observe what happens to waves in a system when the influence of one part of the system on another isn't necessarily reciprocated.

These are known as non-reciprocal interactions, and they can produce some peculiar dynamics. Under the right conditions, rather than settling into a jumble of competing oscillations, waves can gradually reorganize, with longer, slower patterns taking over from shorter, faster ones.
Eventually, a single coherent rhythm can emerge across the entire system.
To show that this can happen mathematically is one thing – but manifesting it in a real material is a bit trickier.
For this, the researchers built an unusual metamaterial – one whose properties emerge from its structure, rather than its composition.
It consisted of 37 units arranged in a honeycomb-like lattice, each made from three elastic hexagons fitted with sensors, actuators, and a tiny electronic controller.

The components were programmed to respond to one another in a very particular way. When one hexagon was compressed, its clockwise neighbor compressed too, while its counterclockwise neighbor expanded.
This asymmetrical response allowed the researchers to engineer the non-reciprocal interactions they wanted to study.
They gave the honeycomb a nudge, introducing small, random disturbances into the structure, and watched what happened.

At first, the individual units began vibrating rapidly, at around 30 times per second. But gradually, larger waves emerged, traveling around the material's edge, overwhelming the smaller oscillations.
Then, as the waves grew longer, their oscillations slowed until the entire honeycomb was moving together in a single, synchronized rhythm.
Anyone can make a wave, though. The next part is demonstrating that the wave is a time crystal.
For that, the researchers needed to establish that the synchronized oscillations weren't just a fleeting phenomenon, but a form of order that could persist even when jostled by random disturbances.
They turned to mathematical analysis and computer simulations, introducing noise into their model to see whether it would destroy the synchronized rhythm.
It didn't. Their results showed that the oscillations could remain coherent despite the disturbances, even as the system approached an effectively infinite size.

The honeycomb wasn't the end of the experiments, either. The researchers wanted to know if the effect could emerge in a system with a different architecture – so they built a donut for waves to ride, like an extraordinarily weird mechanical bull crossed with air hockey.

It consisted of a single elastic ring fitted with 24 motors, programmed to produce non-reciprocal interactions between neighboring sections. They placed it on an air table, allowing it to float with minimal friction.
When they activated the motors and disturbed the ring, waves began to travel around its circumference, deforming it into a succession of shifting polygonal shapes.
As the waves grew longer and slower, the polygons developed fewer sides, until the ring's motion was dominated by a single large-scale pattern.
The researchers did not separately establish that this system also formed a time crystal, but it did reveal something important about wave coarsening.

Their mathematical analysis showed that, as the waves grow in amplitude, they change the dynamics of the system, increasingly favoring waves with longer wavelengths. Those larger waves then grow stronger, further shifting the balance in their favor.
This creates a feedback loop in which the dominant waves become progressively larger and slower, until they reach the limits imposed by the size of the material itself.
Rather than having to impose a synchronized rhythm from outside, the researchers found a way for the material to organize its own vibrations.
Finally, there was one more surprise. The researchers also found that the process could be interrupted.

In their mathematical model, adding friction changed which waves were able to grow. The longest waves were suppressed, preventing the vibrations from continuing to reorganize into ever-larger patterns.
Instead of the entire material falling into step, the system could settle into a different kind of order – persistent waves traveling in one direction along its edge.

This suggests that the same underlying physics could produce different kinds of organized motion, depending on the conditions. By understanding how to control those conditions, researchers may eventually find new ways to guide vibrations through engineered materials.
The discovery could have implications for fields ranging from acoustics to soft robotics, although practical applications remain some way off.

But perhaps the most exciting part is that the researchers didn't need to induce and guide the rhythm of the material's vibrations. By engineering how its components interacted, they created conditions in which the vibrations could organize themselves.
Their results suggest that this self-organization could offer a new route to the robust, long-lasting temporal order that has proved so difficult to achieve in time crystals.

"We anticipate that wave coarsening represents an exemplary route towards time-crystallization in systems with additional symmetries and associated Goldstone modes," they write, "which can be leveraged as a control strategy for shape changes and directed motion in fields such as robotics, active matter and optomechanics with non-reciprocal phase transitions."
The research has been published in Nature.

articles.title: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

paras.en: Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

- The aging brain may be undergoing a remarkable transformation rather than simply losing its abilities, shifting its focus from remembering details to understanding the bigger picture. Scientists suggest this change could be an evolutionary adaptation that helps older adults develop wisdom and share decades of knowledge with younger generations.

Growing older is often associated with memory loss and declining mental abilities. However, scientists are questioning whether these changes tell the whole story. Rather than simply becoming less capable, the brain may be adapting to a new stage of life in which accumulated knowledge, wisdom, and understanding become more important than remembering every detail.

Researchers at the University of Arizona have proposed a different way of understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on findings from molecular biology and brain imaging, they suggest that the changes occurring in older brains may reflect a natural stage of human development rather than deterioration alone. Their work, published in Perspectives on Psychological Science, offers a new perspective on why thinking and memory change with age.

The researchers call their proposed explanation the adaptive aging hypothesis. It suggests that the brain gradually adjusts its priorities to make better use of a lifetime of accumulated experience. This could help explain why older adults often have valuable strengths in teaching, mentoring, storytelling, and passing knowledge to younger generations.

"If we look at normative aging as a story of just decline, we are really missing the boat," said study coauthor Fabian-Xosé Fernandez, an associate professor of cognition and neural systems at the University of Arizona. "The older brain is optimized for different things than the younger brain, predominantly the sharing of stored expertise and social relationships."
How the Brain Shifts From Memory to Meaning

Two brain regions play important roles in how people remember and interpret their experiences. The hippocampus helps preserve specific information about events, including their details and circumstances. The frontal cortex, meanwhile, is more involved in extracting broader meaning, recognizing patterns, and understanding the central message of an experience, sometimes called its "gist."

According to the researchers, the balance between these systems changes during healthy aging. As people grow older, the brain tends to place less emphasis on activity in the hippocampus and rely more on the frontal cortex. This shift may allow the brain to focus more on interpreting information through existing knowledge rather than recording every new experience in precise detail.

"The fact that you see this across people and animal models suggests there is an evolutionary driving force," Fernandez said. "One could argue you are developing your entire life, and development occurs in lockstep with the needs of your brain. When you're younger, the hippocampus turns on because you don't have a knowledge base or know how the world works. A kid absorbs information like a sponge because they are building an archive of information. In early life, the balance is tilted toward recollecting declarative memories with precision, detail, and context."

paras.en: Young brains need to gather enormous amounts of new information because they are still building a foundation for understanding the world. By later adulthood, however, people have already developed extensive stores of memories, concepts, and experiences. Connecting new information to what they already know may become more useful than retaining every individual detail.

The researchers suggest that this changing balance reflects a shift in how the brain processes experience. Instead of concentrating primarily on collecting detailed memories, it increasingly emphasizes understanding relationships, identifying underlying meaning, and applying previously acquired knowledge.
Why Evolution May Favor Wisdom in Older Adults

Evidence of similar changes in animal models raises the possibility that this transition has an evolutionary explanation. Fernandez suggests that the aging brain may be adapting to help individuals preserve and share the knowledge they have acquired throughout their lives.

From this perspective, the ability to draw on decades of experience could be especially valuable for making judgments, guiding others, and transferring important information between generations. Older adults may therefore play a distinct role in supporting younger people through mentorship, teaching, and storytelling.

"Given those goals, it makes sense that you aren't interested in nitty-gritty details," Fernandez said. "You are interested in safeguarding the vast knowledge you already have. Evolution may be saying that if you make it long enough, there's a need to transmit this information, so we put into motion biological changes that enforce and protect your semantic and autobiographical memories."

Under this hypothesis, changes in memory and thinking are not necessarily signs that the brain is functioning less effectively. They may instead reflect a different set of priorities, with greater emphasis on preserving meaningful knowledge and using it to understand new situations.
Why Healthy Brain Aging Is Different From Alzheimer's
The adaptive aging hypothesis could also provide scientists with another way to examine the differences between normal cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease.

Although both involve changes in memory, Fernandez emphasizes that Alzheimer's should not be understood as ordinary aging taken to an extreme. The biological processes involved are fundamentally different.
"When I was in grad school, people thought about Alzheimer's as a more intense version of cognitive aging, but that is just not the case," Fernandez said. "They are completely different."

During typical aging, the brain's gradual shift away from relying heavily on the hippocampus and toward greater involvement of the frontal cortex generally unfolds between the fifth and seventh decades of life. In Alzheimer's disease, however, abnormal processes involving proteins such as amyloid and tau may interfere with this transition.

One important distinction involves activity in the hippocampus. While healthy aging is generally associated with reduced emphasis on this region, Alzheimer's can involve unusually high levels of hippocampal activity. Rather than supporting the normal progression of cognitive development, disease-related changes may disrupt the brain networks responsible for memory and understanding.

"In normative aging, hippocampal activation is deemphasized, which is probably what should be happening in a 70-year-old. But in many cases of Alzheimer's, it turns out the hippocampus is hyperactive," he said. "This beautiful developmental transition is completely disrupted in Alzheimer's disease by pathological processes that mess with episodic memory and interfere with circuits that allow you to think about your own life, lexicon, and vocabulary."

These disruptions can affect the ability to recall personal experiences and access stored knowledge, including words and their meanings. Understanding how these changes differ from the adaptations associated with healthy aging may help researchers develop a clearer picture of normal brain development and neurodegenerative disease.
Embracing the Hidden Strengths of the Aging Brain

The researchers argue that society may need to reconsider what successful brain aging looks like. Encouraging older adults to process information exactly as younger people do may not always be the most productive approach.

Fernandez suggests that placing excessive emphasis on remembering precise details could work against the brain's changing priorities. "For many individuals, the weight of how you process information should probably not be so hippocampal-centric by the sixth or seventh decade."

Instead of judging older adults primarily by abilities that tend to weaken with age, the researchers encourage greater recognition of the capabilities that may become especially valuable later in life.

Creating more opportunities for social interaction could be one way to support these strengths. Relationships between older and younger generations may be particularly beneficial because they provide opportunities to exchange experiences, share expertise, and preserve knowledge that might otherwise be lost.

"People see older individuals and look at them as not being on par with younger individuals across a lot of metrics," Fernandez says. "The way I look at it is that you've got someone with a brain that has been active for several decades and has seen a lot. There is tremendous value there, and we don't do a good job of unlocking it."

The central message of the adaptive aging hypothesis is that growing older may involve more than a gradual reduction in cognitive abilities. Although some mental skills become less reliable with age, the brain may also be adapting to make better use of the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime. Recognizing those strengths could change how society understands aging and the contributions older adults can make.

articles.title: Scientists discover a way to kill dangerous gut bacteria without killing the good

paras.en: Scientists discover a way to kill dangerous gut bacteria without killing the good
- Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research

- Scientists have discovered a natural compound that targets dangerous C. difficile bacteria without wiping out the gut's beneficial microbes. Successful early tests suggest it could lead to a gentler, more effective treatment for stubborn intestinal infections that frequently return.

A dangerous intestinal infection may soon have a more targeted treatment option. Scientists have identified a natural compound that can kill the bacteria responsible for severe gut infections while leaving much of the beneficial gut microbiome unharmed.

The bacterium Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) is naturally found in the intestines of many people and generally causes no problems when present in small amounts. However, antibiotics that target a wide range of bacteria can upset the delicate balance of microorganisms in the gut. This disruption allows C. difficile to multiply rapidly, potentially causing severe intestinal inflammation that can become chronic.

C. difficile infections (CDI) are among the leading causes of diarrhea associated with antibiotic treatment. The bacteria produce toxins that can trigger dangerous and sometimes life-threatening inflammation in the intestines. Because these infections frequently return after treatment, scientists are searching for more effective ways to eliminate the pathogen without causing additional damage to the gut microbiome.

A team led by Prof. Rolf Müller, department head and scientific director at HIPS, has now identified a promising drug candidate that specifically targets C. difficile while preserving much of the gut's beneficial microbial community. HIPS is a site of the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI) that operates in collaboration with Saarland University.
Natural Compound Targets Dangerous Gut Bacteria

The researchers found that argyrin B, a naturally occurring antibacterial substance, was highly effective against C. difficile in laboratory tests and experiments involving infected mice. Importantly, the compound showed little activity against the beneficial microorganisms that help maintain a healthy digestive system.

"We were able to show that the natural compound argyrin B is highly effective against CDI: both in laboratory experiments and in a mouse model of the infection, where it significantly reduces the bacterial load," says Dr. Jennifer Herrmann, senior scientist in the department "Microbial Natural Products" at HIPS. "An antibacterial target of the argyrins had previously been identified and characterized in the notorious hospital-acquired pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Now we have been able to show that argyrin B also acts on this target in C. difficile and exhibits particularly high efficacy in doing so. In contrast, the argyrins have virtually no effect on the beneficial microorganisms in our digestive tract. The gut microbiome could therefore be spared during treatment with argyrin and restored to a healthy state more quickly."

paras.en: A Bacteria-Killing Substance Found in Soil
Argyrins were originally discovered in myxobacteria, microorganisms that inhabit soil. These bacteria produce natural substances that help them attack other microbes and use them as a source of food.

Although argyrin B has demonstrated promising antibacterial activity, researchers must also determine whether its pharmaceutical properties make it suitable for use as a medicine. That includes understanding how the compound behaves inside the body and whether it could cause unwanted effects.

One particularly encouraging finding emerged when the team examined what happens after mice receive argyrin B orally. Very little of the compound entered their bloodstream. Instead, most of it remained in the large intestine, where C. difficile infections occur.

By concentrating in the gut rather than circulating throughout the body, argyrin B could potentially reduce the risk of side effects affecting other organs. Together with its selective activity against C. difficile, this characteristic makes the compound a promising candidate for a treatment that may be better tolerated.
Could It Help Prevent Recurring Gut Infections?

One of the biggest challenges in treating C. difficile is its tendency to return. Patients who experience multiple relapses are often treated using fecal microbiota transfer (commonly known as a stool transplant). This procedure aims to restore a healthier balance of gut microorganisms, but it can be complicated to perform and unpleasant for patients.

A medication developed from argyrin could eventually provide another treatment option. By eliminating the harmful bacteria without extensively disrupting the rest of the microbiome, such a therapy might reduce the likelihood of further infections and relapses. That could also help some patients avoid the need for stool transplants.

More research is needed before argyrin B can be considered for clinical use. The scientists plan to investigate which dosage produces the strongest antibacterial effect and use additional experimental models to determine whether the compound can also combat recurring C. difficile infections.
